overview.before:
A person uses the World ID app to authenticate with their World ID. The World ID
issuer verifies that authentication and issues a signed ID token to your backend.
Your application uses the token to recognize the same World ID and determine when the person last
authenticated. Your application keeps its own accounts, sessions, permissions,
and actions.
overview.after:
The World ID issuer returns a signed ID token through OpenID Connect (OIDC).
Your application controls its accounts, sessions, permissions, and actions.

registration.before:
Sign in to the [developer portal](https://auth.world.org/portal) with Google to register an
OIDC client for your application or auth server. This registration supports
step-up, human-in-the-loop workflows, and primary sign-in.
registration.after:
Register an OIDC client for your application or auth server in the
[developer portal](https://auth.world.org/portal).

registration.before:
Developers sign in to the portal with Google to manage clients. Your users
authenticate with World ID in your application.

Your coding agent can [read the public integration guides](/world-id-auth/build-with-a-coding-agent#give-your-coding-agent-the-guide)
without a plugin or MCP connection. Optionally
[connect developer MCP tools](/world-id-auth/build-with-a-coding-agent#connect-your-coding-agent)
to register and manage the application. Portal tools use Google authorization, and registration
and credential changes require your approval in the portal. Keep client secrets
and private keys outside agent conversations. The
[agent instructions](/world-id-auth/coding-agent-reference.md) cover portal tool use.
registration.after: For optional registration and app management, [connect your coding agent](/world-id-auth/build-with-a-coding-agent). Registration and credential changes require your approval in the portal.

browser.before:
Connect your backend to the World ID issuer with OpenID Connect (OIDC). Your backend receives
a signed ID token and validates it before using the account identifier and
authentication time. Step-up, human checkpoints, and primary sign-in all use this
connection.
browser.after: Connect your backend to the World ID issuer with OpenID Connect (OIDC).

browser.before:
1. **Start authorization.** Redirect the browser to the discovered authorization
   endpoint with `client_id`, the exact registered `redirect_uri`,
   `response_type=code`, `scope=openid`, a fresh `state`, an optional fresh
   `nonce`, and an S256 PKCE challenge. Keep the PKCE verifier in your server-side
   state for this attempt.
2. **Handle the callback.** The World ID issuer handles passkey or World ID proof authentication and
   browser-session eligibility, then redirects to your callback. Validate the
   returned `state` and require the response's `iss` parameter to match the
   discovered issuer exactly before redeeming the code. Success and error
   responses both include `iss`. Treat an authorization error as a failure,
   never as success.
3. **Exchange the code.** POST the code to the discovered token endpoint,
   authenticated with your [registered method](/world-id-auth/connect-your-backend#client-authentication).
   Each code can be used once and expires after five minutes.
4. **Validate the ID token** as described in
   [Validate the ID token](/world-id-auth/connect-your-backend#validate-the-id-token),
   then find the account by `(iss, sub)`.
browser.after:
Save fresh `state`, an optional fresh `nonce`, and the S256 PKCE verifier in
server-side state for each attempt. On success and error callbacks, validate
`state` and require `iss` to match the discovered issuer before redeeming the code.
Treat authorization errors as failure. Exchange the code with your registered
client-authentication method; each code expires after five minutes and can be
used once. [Validate the ID token](/world-id-auth/connect-your-backend#validate-the-id-token)
before finding the account by `(iss, sub)`.

identity.before:
For example, if a user authenticates at 10:00 and their existing session produces
a token at 11:00, `auth_time` still represents 10:00 while `iat` represents 11:00.
Use `auth_time` for authentication freshness, as described in
[Step-up authentication](/world-id-auth/step-up).

federation.before:
Connect the World ID issuer to the auth server used by your MCP server. Your auth
server validates the issuer's ID token and maps `(iss, sub)` to your application's
account. This lets you associate MCP activity with the same account across
sessions. Your auth server issues access tokens, and your MCP server controls
access to its tools. The MCP client is the software connecting the agent to your
server.
federation.after:
Connect the World ID issuer to the auth server used by your MCP server. The MCP
client is the software connecting the agent to your server.

federation.before:
The diagram shows which service issues and receives each token. Browser
authorization uses two code exchanges:

- **World ID issuer → your auth server:** the issuer redirects the user's browser
  to your auth server's callback with a code. Your auth server exchanges it for
  an ID token and validates the result.
- **Your auth server → the MCP client:** after checking permissions and required
  consent, your auth server redirects the browser to the MCP client's callback
  with a different code. The client exchanges it for an access token for your
  MCP server.
federation.after:
Browser authorization uses two separate code exchanges. Your auth server
exchanges the World ID code for an ID token. After permission and consent checks,
it sends a different code to the MCP client's callback; the client exchanges it
for an access token for your MCP server.

xaa.before:
World IdP supports consumer-controlled identity delegation using
[ID-JAG](https://www.ietf.org/archive/id/draft-ietf-oauth-identity-assertion-authz-grant-04.html).
A user connects an agent host and chooses the apps it may access. The host can
then obtain credentials for those apps without separate World ID authentication
for each app. Each app's authorization server issues its own access tokens and
controls API permissions. The app does not need OIDC sign-in federation.
xaa.after:
Use [ID-JAG](https://www.ietf.org/archive/id/draft-ietf-oauth-identity-assertion-authz-grant-04.html)
for user-controlled access from an agent host to your application's MCP server.
The app does not need OIDC sign-in federation.

xaa.before:
This guide covers app integration and user permissions. The host's MCP
authentication layer handles World sign-in, ID-JAG exchange, token renewal,
and credential storage. The model calls MCP tools and can help developers
implement the integration. Credentials stay outside model context, tool results,
and conversations.

agent-setup.before:
Connect a coding agent to the World ID developer tools. No plugin is required.
The public integration guides are available without sign-in or an MCP connection.
Add the developer MCP server only when you want the agent to register or manage
your application through tools.
agent-setup.after:
Use these public guides with your coding agent. Connect the developer MCP server
only for application management.

agent-setup.before:
Keep the connection, guides, app registration, and credentials in the same
production or sandbox environment. Before authorizing, confirm that the current
session lists the developer MCP server at `https://auth.world.org/mcp/developer`.
Call `list_idp_guides` to check the connection; it requires no authorization.
agent-setup.after:
Keep the connection, guides, app registration, and credentials in the same
production or sandbox environment.

agent-setup.before: Complete Google sign-in and consent in the browser when authorizing portal access.

If the tools are unavailable, first check whether the developer server is listed
and enabled in the active host. Add it only if it is missing; otherwise use the
host's refresh controls. Start a new coding session if the host needs one to load
new tools. A desktop or workspace host manages its own connection; configuring a
separate CLI does not establish that the active chat can use it.

Ask the agent to list the World ID integration guides to confirm the connection.
Reading guides requires no authorization. For app management, ask the agent to
check developer access and follow the Google sign-in and portal consent prompt.

testing.before: Use the checks that apply to your integration and authorization policy.
